blocks.x: Omnichannel retail wins on promise-keeping: availability, delivery promise, price consistency and service resolution across channels. The decision infrastructure behind those promises — demand sensing, allocation, pricing — decides margin before marketing spends a cent. This page is the operating picture: what runs, what strains, and which capabilities move the numbers that decide the margin.

The work concentrates in demand sensing and pricing, allocation/replenishment, order promise and fulfillment, with shelf operations close behind. Volume grows on every path; the decision layer has not kept up. That gap is measurable, and it is the work.
What the operations floor feels every week
named from the floor, not from a framework, Omnichannel Retail edition:

items: Forecasts update weekly while baskets shift daily; markdowns and stockouts both inherit the lag.
Store/DC allocation on legacy rules; phantom availability coexists with overstock.
OOS and planogram drift discovered at audit; camera estates idle.
Consent and profiling governance is not yet defined; personalization ships as generic segments.
Trading peaks break cost and reliability models; P95 cost per order unknown.
Account takeover drains points and trust; controls static.

blocks.x: The proof in Omnichannel Retail is a working system on a real workflow. These are the builds that go live:

items: streaming signals into daily SKU-store forecasts
size-curve and DC logic proposed to planners

blocks.x: What the regime expects of you
Gdpr/ccpa — profiling and consent duties. Programs here are designed against these duties from the first sprint; evidence is a by-product of running the system, not an audit-season project.

blocks.caption: Regimes in scope for Omnichannel Retail

blocks.x: For Omnichannel Retail, the first move costs little: a two-week diagnostic on demand signals batch-stale, your data, one honest baseline. The scoped proposal only follows if the measured delta justifies it.
Talk to the team that runs operations in Omnichannel Retail in production — the briefing is technical by design, and the first one costs nothing but the hour.
